## Dry-carry of passive tracers, and the zero-base guard {#sec-ch08-drycarry}

<!-- PROVENANCE
pin: snapy@919936da07d80a310b98ab11da184972a3203274 (chengcli/snapy)
sources: OUTLINE.md 8.13
status: draft
-->

### Summary

This is the one entry in the chapter that is not about positivity at all. The distinction is worth making loudly
because its name and its neighbours both suggest otherwise. It keeps an arithmetic expression finite. The tracer it
protects can still go negative, and the repository's own test for it accepts a negative value.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Carry the passive tracers with a dry-mass source, and keep the carried ratio finite at a zero base.

**Data.** In: the dry source, `scalar_r`, the step-start and stage states, the stage weights. Out: an addition to `scalar_ds`.

**Placement.** In `advance_local`, after the native forcings and again after the user callbacks (@sec-ch01-stage).

**Activation.** Scalars present and a forcing that writes dry mass; no switch of its own.

**Guarantee / limits.** Finiteness only: the tracer may legitimately end negative under a dry sink.

**Evidence.** `[C9]` of this chapter's check; `test_dry_carry_zero_base_python` and `test_stage_forcing_dry_tracer_python` ($10^{-12}$).
:::

### Derivation

A forcing that writes a dry-mass tendency has to say what happens to the tracers riding on that mass. Addition and
removal are not symmetric, and the code comment at `carry_dry_source`
({{< code src/mesh/meshblock.cpp MeshBlockImpl::advance_local >}}) gives the reason. An addition carries the ratio as
it stands at source entry. A removal carries the ratio the stage would have had with no source at all. So the removal
cannot amplify a ratio that transport or the implicit solve has just changed.

Computing that source-free ratio means dividing the source-free scalar by the source-free density. Nothing prevents
that density from being zero in a cell that is empty with the source removed. The guard at `rho_base`
({{< code src/mesh/meshblock.cpp MeshBlockImpl::advance_local >}}) substitutes the entry ratio there, which keeps the
expression finite.

What the guard does *not* do is bound the result. The repository's own test asserts a finite answer at a
zero base and accepts a bottom value of $-5\times10^{-4}$: a negative tracer is the expected outcome,
not a failure. Passive scalars under a dry sink have no positivity guarantee from this path or from any
other.

`[C9]` separates the three statements. Over $2\times10^5$ cells the stage moves the ratio away from its entry value by
up to $1.46$, so the two rules are genuinely different. Carrying the source-free ratio rather than the entry one
changes the result by up to $1.16$ of scalar. It is the entry rule that would amplify the ratio transport has just
changed. At a zero source-free density the guard returns the entry ratio and the expression stays finite. It stays
unbounded below all the same: under a dry sink $66\,587$ of the $2\times10^5$ cells end with a negative scalar, worst
$-1.4$ [check `src/snapy_report/ch08/checks/positivity_check.py`, output `src/snapy_report/ch08/checks/positivity_check.out`].

### Numerical method

The carry is the lambda at `scalar_r` ({{< code src/mesh/meshblock.cpp MeshBlockImpl::advance_local >}}). The
source-free density and scalar are rebuilt by running the integrator's own stage combination on the tendency with the
dry source subtracted at `rho_base` ({{< code src/mesh/meshblock.cpp MeshBlockImpl::advance_local >}}). So the
"source-free" state is the one the integrator would have produced. It is not a cell-wise approximation of it. The
choice between the two ratios is made per cell on the sign of the dry source at `carry_r`
({{< code src/mesh/meshblock.cpp MeshBlockImpl::advance_local >}}).

**Why two ratios, and why no bound.** Three facts of the code.

1. An addition carries the ratio at source entry; a removal carries the ratio the stage would have had with no source,
   rebuilt with the integrator's own combination. So a removal cannot amplify a ratio transport has just changed
   ({{< code src/mesh/meshblock.cpp MeshBlockImpl::advance_local >}}).
2. The source-free ratio divides by the source-free density, which can be zero in an emptied cell; the guard
   substitutes the entry ratio there and the expression stays finite.
3. Nothing bounds the outcome below: `[C9]` finds $66\,587$ of $2\times10^5$ cells negative under a dry sink, worst
   $-1.4$, and the repository's own test asserts a negative value.

: Code map of the dry-carry guard. {#tbl-ch08-drycarry-code}

**How to use it.** Nothing is set: any forcing that writes a dry-mass increment, native or scripted, goes through
the carry when scalars exist. The two rules and the guard are these lines
({{< code src/mesh/meshblock.cpp MeshBlockImpl::advance_local >}}):

```cpp
    auto remove_r =
        torch::where(rho_base.unsqueeze(0) == 0., vars.at("scalar_r"),
                     s_base / rho_base.unsqueeze(0));
    auto carry_r =
        torch::where(dry.unsqueeze(0) < 0., remove_r, vars.at("scalar_r"));
    fut_scalar_ds.add_(carry_r * dry.unsqueeze(0));
```

`rho_base` and `s_base` are the source-free stage density and scalar, `dry` the dry source, and the first
`where` is the zero-base guard.

: Tests of the dry-carry guard. {#tbl-ch08-drycarry-tests}

The first test is the clearest statement in the repository that this is not a positivity mechanism: it asserts a
negative value to twelve digits. The chapter's check separates the three statements on synthetic
cells.[^ch08-drycarry-run] `[C9]`: transport moves the ratio from its entry value by up to $1.46$, the two rules
differ by up to $1.16$ of scalar. The guard returns the entry ratio at a zero base, and $66\,587$ of $200\,000$ cells
end negative under a dry sink. The two ctests have not been run for this report at the pin: **pending a pinned ctest
run**.

### Limits

::: {.callout-warning title="Limits"}
- No positivity guarantee for passive scalars under a dry sink. The guard keeps the arithmetic finite
  and nothing more.
:::

1. **A fallback, not a correction.** When the source-free density is zero the entry ratio is used
   instead. Whether that ratio is the physically right one in an emptied cell is not argued anywhere;
   it is the finite choice.
